## 1. Foundations

### Big data primer: the 5 V's

| | What it means | Today | The question it raises |
|---|---|---|---|
| 📦 **Volume** | How much | From about **2 ZB a year in 2010** to roughly **175–200 ZB in 2025** (IDC estimates) | How do we store it? |
| ⚡ **Velocity** | How fast | The world creates around **0.4–0.5 ZB per day**; a growing share is real-time | How fast must we process it? |
| 🧩 **Variety** | How many shapes | Tables, JSON, logs, images, audio… and now **embeddings** for AI | How do we handle every format? |
| 🔍 **Veracity** | How trustworthy | More important than ever: AI amplifies whatever errors are in the data | Can we trust it? |
| 💶 **Value** | Why bother | Data is an **asset**; big data is a must-have capability in every industry | What decision does it improve? |

**Takeaways:** big data is the result of the evolution of **data, technology and BI**. It's not about size alone, but about what the old tools couldn't handle, and there's a vast variety of use cases in every industry. You saw all of the V's in the labs: volume (605,765 flights), velocity (a Binance tick every second), variety (CSV, JSON, WebSocket messages) and veracity (`"NA"` hiding nulls).

### From two Google papers to lakehouses and AI

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 2003 | Google File System paper |
| 2004 | MapReduce paper |
| 2006 | Hadoop born at Yahoo! |
| 2008 | Hadoop becomes an Apache top-level project |
| 2011 | Kafka open-sourced by LinkedIn |
| 2014 | Spark sorts 100 TB **3× faster than Hadoop with 10× fewer machines**; NiFi donated to the ASF |
| 2016 | Spark 2.0 introduces the SparkSession |
| 2020 | The lakehouse: open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg) |
| 2025 | Kafka 4 drops ZooKeeper; Spark 4 makes ANSI SQL the default |
| 2026 | Spark 4.2; big data platforms become the foundation of AI |

**The key idea never changed:** split the data, spread it over many machines, and send the computation to where the data is. Big data started with Hadoop, which was based on Google's papers. Hadoop is legacy today, but HDFS, YARN and MapReduce explain why Spark, Kafka and lakehouses look the way they do. Big data is an **ecosystem** of dozens of technologies.

### Big data today (2026): five shifts

1. **☁️ From clusters to the cloud:** managed services instead of Hadoop clusters. In Q2 2026, Synergy Research put AWS at 28%, Azure at 20% and Google Cloud at 15% of cloud infrastructure.
2. **🧱 Storage and compute apart:** data sits cheaply in **object storage** (S3, MinIO) and engines scale up and down on demand. That's why our labs read `s3a://`.
3. **🏠 Lakehouse and open table formats:** Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi add ACID transactions, schema evolution and time travel to files in the lake.
4. **⚡ Streaming first:** real-time pipelines are mainstream, with Kafka 4 (no ZooKeeper), Flink 2 and Spark Structured Streaming.
5. **🧭 Data mesh and data products:** domain teams own their data and publish it as documented, governed products.
6. **🤖 Big data meets AI:** LLMs, RAG with embeddings and vector search… and **AI-ready data** as the deciding factor. Gartner expects 60% of AI projects without it to be abandoned through 2026.

### Data & files: structure decides the tools

| Structured | Semi-structured | Unstructured |
|---|---|---|
| CSV · TSV · tables | JSON · XML · Avro | text · HTML · images · video · audio · PDF |
| MovieLens, flights | TfL bike points, Binance | |
| schema up front | schema in the data | no schema |

![The TfL BikePoint JSON in the browser: semi-structured data from labs 5.1, 16.1 and 18.1](data:image/webp;base64,)

Data is often stored in files, which come as **text** (CSV, JSON, TXT, HTML) or **binary** (images, video, audio, PDF… and **storage formats**).

One day of TfL bike data, 230,112 rows (lecture 6.2):

| Format | Size |
|---|---|
| JSON | 46.1 MB |
| CSV | 22.4 MB |
| CSV + gzip | 5.7 MB |
| **Parquet** | **0.9 MB** |

Text formats are easy to read and to ingest, so land raw data as it arrives. **Storage formats** (Parquet, ORC, Avro) are binary and built for analytics: **columnar**, compressed, with the schema inside. Parquet was **24× smaller than CSV** and read 2 columns in 0.01 s, versus 0.24 s to load the whole CSV.

## 2. Ingestion

### Data ingestion: the toughest part

Data ingestion is about **capturing and collecting data** and loading or transporting it into the **storage layer**, in batch or as a stream. It's one of the toughest parts of a big data solution.

```
MovieLens CSVs  ┐   🧺 BATCH: data accumulates and moves in chunks, on a schedule      ─► Batch store (HDFS · MinIO / S3: files)
TfL API (JSON)  ├─►    MovieLens once (7.1) · a TfL file every 5 min (15.1) · 1 Binance file/min (7.2)
Flights CSV     │   ⚡ STREAMING: each event moves as soon as it happens               ─► Streaming store (Kafka: events)
Binance ticks   ┘      a Binance miniTicker every second → topic binance.bitcoin (8.2)
```

- **Why so hard?** Many sources, variable **speed** and **variety**, unreliable networks, credentials, and formats that change.
- **No single tool:** we often need **several technologies**, depending on the data source and the latency required.
- **Start from requirements:** latency, source type, volume, platform, team skills and cost. Then pick NiFi, Airflow, CDC, managed connectors…

### Apache NiFi: data flows you can see

Apache NiFi is an **easy-to-use, powerful and reliable** system to process and distribute data that addresses the challenges of **enterprise data ingestion at scale**.

![The TfL flow running in NiFi 2 (labs 5.1 and 16.1): six processors from the API to MinIO](data:image/webp;base64,)

| Concept | What it is |
|---|---|
| **FlowFile** | a piece of data: content + attributes (`filename`, `${now()}`…) |
| **Processor** | does one job: `InvokeHTTP`, `SplitJson`, `PutHDFS`, `PutS3Object`, `PublishKafka` |
| **Connection** | a queue between processors, with back pressure |
| **Process Group** | a reusable sub-flow, exported as a JSON *flow definition* |
| **Controller Service** | shared configuration: credentials, SSL, WebSocket client |
| **Provenance** | the full history of every FlowFile |

> ⚠ **Lesson from the labs:** sensitive values are **not exported** with a flow, so after every import you add the keys again in the controller services.

## 3. Storage

### Two stores, two jobs

Almost every big data solution requires both a **batch data store** and a **streaming data store**.

| | 🗂️ Batch storage | 🌊 Streaming storage |
|---|---|---|
| Kind | **file-based** | **event-based** |
| Strength | **volume + variety** | **velocity + variety** |
| Role | Maybe the most important one, because it stores **all** the data. It must be carefully designed to enforce **security, data quality and governance**. | Eases and speeds up **real-time processing**. Events that enter this way are **also stored in the batch store**. |
| Technologies | HDFS, MinIO, Amazon S3, Parquet, Delta Lake | Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar |

![Object storage in practice: the raw-flights bucket in MinIO (lab 17.1)](data:image/webp;base64,)

In lab 8.2, a single NiFi flow fed **both** stores: one file per minute to MinIO and every tick to Kafka.

### A data lake you can navigate

We stored data following a **data lake** approach, directly in HDFS (lab 8.1), with the HDFS command-line interface, and in MinIO (labs 8.2, 16.1–18.1). Datasets are organised in directory trees following the pattern **`/<layer>/<source>/<dataset>/…`**:

| Layer | Purpose | Examples from the course |
|---|---|---|
| 🥉 **raw · bronze** | as it arrived, never edited, replayable | `/datalake/raw/movielens/movies/movies.csv` (HDFS, lab 8.1) · `s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_yyyyMMdd_hhmm.json` (labs 16.1, 18.1) · `s3a://raw-binance/…` (lab 8.2) · `s3a://raw-flights/flights_jan08.csv` (lab 17.1) |
| 🥈 **curated · silver** | cleaned, typed, deduplicated, Parquet partitioned by date | `/curated/tfl/bikepoints/dt=2026-11-07/` · `/curated/dot/flights/` read with `nullValue="NA"` |
| 🥇 **analytics · gold** | aggregated, business-ready | `bikepoint_stats` (min/max/avg) · `delays_by_origin_airport` |

A **lakehouse table format** (Delta Lake, Iceberg or Hudi over Parquet) adds ACID transactions, schema evolution and time travel. Names, not tools, make a lake navigable; without them, it becomes a **data swamp**.

### HDFS and Kafka in one picture each

```
HDFS · big files, split and replicated                    Kafka · an ordered, replayable log of events
ratings_big.csv (300 MB) → B1 128 · B2 128 · B3 44 MB      NiFi PublishKafka ─produce─► topic binance.bitcoin
NameNode: metadata (blocks → DataNodes)                       P0: [0][1][2][3]…     ─► group A (console) at offset 3
DataNode 1: B1 B3 · DataNode 2: B1 B2                         P1: [0][1][2]…        ─► group B (Spark) at offset 1
DataNode 3: B2 B3 · DataNode 4: B1 B2 (+ B3 copies)           P2: [0][1][2][3][4]…
128 MB blocks · 3 replicas · throughput over latency       append-only · ordered per partition · Kafka 4: KRaft, no ZooKeeper
```

## 4. Processing

### The right engine for each job

Processing is about **how we transform the data**. Different technologies in the ecosystem cover different scenarios, depending on processing velocity and analytical goals.

| Type | Goal | Technologies (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| 🧺 Batch | process large, finished datasets | Spark · MapReduce (legacy) |
| ⚡ Stream | react to events within seconds | Flink 2 · Spark Structured Streaming · Kafka Streams |
| 🔄 ETL / ELT | extract, clean, reshape, load | PySpark · Databricks Lakeflow · dbt |
| 🧾 SQL | query the lake with SQL | Hive 4 · Trino · Spark SQL · DuckDB · BigQuery · Snowflake |
| 🕸️ Graph | relationships, paths, communities | GraphFrames · Neo4j |
| 🧠 ML / AI | train models, embeddings, RAG | Spark MLlib · Databricks · vector search |
| 🗓️ Workflow managers | schedule and chain all of the above | Airflow 3 · Kestra (in OSBDET) |

**Takeaway:** Apache **Spark** and Apache **Flink** are the most versatile processing technologies today; Apache **Hive** is one of the oldest and most relevant technologies for SQL processing.

### Hadoop and MapReduce: move the code, not the data

Hadoop is a technology for **storing and processing massive volumes of data**, based on original ideas from Google's papers. Its key idea is to **drive computation to where the data is stored**. It has three components:

- **HDFS:** distributed, file-based storage, optimised for large files (128–256 MB blocks): high throughput at the expense of latency.
- **YARN:** the cluster operating system. It manages and balances CPU and memory between running applications, and lets other engines (such as Spark) run on a Hadoop cluster.
- **MapReduce:** distributed **batch-only** processing that chains map and reduce steps, Hadoop's implementation of Google's model.

Hadoop is still maintained (3.5 is current, and OSBDET ships 3.4), but it's considered **legacy**.

**Lab 10.1: movies per genre with Hadoop Streaming**

```
MAP (per line)                  SHUFFLE & SORT (by key)        REDUCE (sum)
Toy Story (1995) → Adventure 1  Action   1 1 1 …               Drama     4361
                   Animation 1  Comedy   1 1 1 …               Comedy    3756
                   Comedy 1 …   Drama    1 1 1 …               Thriller  1894
Heat (1995) → Action 1, Crime 1, Thriller 1 …                  Action    1828 · Romance 1596 … 20 genres
genres-mapper.py (rsplit(",", 1))                              genres-reducer.py
```

Every MapReduce job is **map → shuffle → reduce**, reading from and writing to disk at every step. It's simple and robust, but slow for anything iterative. That's what Spark fixed.

### Apache Spark: one engine, many workloads

Apache Spark is an open-source **unified processing** technology for big data, with several advantages over earlier technologies such as Hadoop. It **unifies multiple processing types in one API**: batch, streaming, ETL, SQL, graph processing and machine learning.

```
Spark SQL / DataFrames · Structured Streaming · MLlib · GraphFrames
Spark Core · RDDs (scheduling, memory, fault tolerance)
Cluster manager: standalone · YARN · Kubernetes
Data: HDFS · S3 · MinIO · Kafka · Parquet · Delta · JDBC…
```

Spark is a **distributed** technology. It relies on **cluster managers** to get resources (memory and CPUs), and a Spark application is made of:

- **Driver** (the brain, one per application): controls the application lifecycle, builds the plan (DAG), splits it into tasks and asks the cluster manager for resources to allocate the executors.
- **Executors** (the muscle, many, on workers): run the tasks the driver demands and cache data in memory.
- **SparkSession:** the first thing we need in any Spark application to start interacting with Spark.

Spark is in its 4.x series (4.2 was released in July 2026); OSBDET ships 3.5.

### The Spark Data API: two levels, two kinds of operation

| | High-level API | Low-level API |
|---|---|---|
| Abstraction | distributed **tables**: DataFrames, Datasets (Scala/Java), SQL | distributed **collections**: RDDs + broadcasts and accumulators |
| Entry point | `SparkSession` | `SparkContext` (inside the session) |
| Notes | relies internally on the low-level API; optimised by Catalyst | for the few things DataFrames can't express |

Both APIs have two types of operation:

- **Transformations are lazy:** `read`, `where`, `select`, `groupBy`… build a plan and return a "new", virtual version of the data abstraction. Nothing runs yet.
- **Actions are eager:** `count`, `collect`, `show`, `toPandas`, `write` fire the computation of every transformation in the chain, partition by partition, on the executors.

> ⚠ **Driver memory:** `collect()` and `toPandas()` bring everything to the driver, so call `limit()` first.

### What Spark really did: jobs, stages, shuffles

![Spark UI, job 0: one reduceByKey creates two stages joined by a shuffle](data:image/webp;base64,)

![Spark UI, Jobs tab: movies per genre three ways (RDD, DataFrame, SQL)](data:image/webp;base64,)

- A **job** is one action. A **stage** is the work between two shuffles. A **task** is one stage running on one partition.
- "**Skipped**" stages mean Spark reused shuffle files it already had.
- The UI (`localhost:24040`) is your best debugging friend: if a job is slow, look for big shuffles and skewed tasks.

### The DataFrames API on one page

We learnt to manipulate DataFrames in many ways. DataFrames provide many functions to transform and act on their data, Spark ships a library with dozens of column functions, and we can write our own **UDFs** (user-defined functions).

| Area | Key methods |
|---|---|
| 🏗️ **Creation** | `spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema)` · `spark.read.csv / json / parquet` · `.option("header", True)` · `schema="userId INT, …"` |
| 🔍 **Inspection** | `printSchema()` · `dtypes` · `columns` · `show()` · `head()` · `limit(n)` · `count()` · `describe()` · `summary()` |
| 🧱 **Columns** | `select` · `withColumn` · `withColumnRenamed` · `drop` · `F.col` · `F.lit` · `alias` · `cast` |
| 🔎 **Rows** | `where / filter` · `distinct` · `orderBy` · `sort` · `limit` · `sample(0.1, seed=42)` |
| 🧮 **Column functions** | boolean `isNull · isin · between` · numeric `round · abs · pow` · string `split · regexp · trim · upper` · date `to_date · year · datediff` · array `explode · size · array_contains` |
| 🛠️ **UDFs** | `@F.udf("string")` (row by row) · `@pandas_udf` (vectorised, Arrow) · prefer built-ins: about 10× faster or more |
| Σ **Aggregation · joins** | `groupBy().agg(min, max, avg)` · `pivot · rollup · cube` · `join(other, "id", "left")` · `broadcast(small_df)` |
| 🕳️ **Nulls · sets** | `dropna · fillna · na.replace` · `F.coalesce · isNotNull` · `union · unionByName` · `intersect · exceptAll` |

Every DataFrame is **immutable**: each method returns a new one.

### One question, four ways: movies per genre

**MapReduce (lab 10.1):**
```python
# genres-mapper.py
for line in sys.stdin:
    genres = line.rsplit(",", 1)[-1]
    for genre in genres.strip().split("|"):
        print(f"{genre}\t1")
# genres-reducer.py sums the 1s per sorted key; run both with hadoop jar … streaming -mapper -reducer
```

**RDD:**
```python
(sc.textFile("movies.csv")
   .filter(lambda l: not l.startswith("movieId"))
   .flatMap(lambda l: [(g, 1) for g in l.rsplit(",", 1)[-1].split("|")])
   .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))
```

**DataFrame:**
```python
(spark.read.option("header", True).csv("movies.csv")
   .select(F.explode(F.split("genres", r"\|")).alias("genre"))
   .groupBy("genre").count()
   .orderBy(F.desc("count")))
```

**SQL:**
```python
movies_df.createOrReplaceTempView("movies")
spark.sql("""
SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM movies LATERAL VIEW explode(split(genres, '[|]')) t AS genre
GROUP BY genre ORDER BY n DESC""")
```

```
Drama 4361 · Comedy 3756 · Thriller 1894 · Action 1828 · Romance 1596    # all four ways agree
```

We went from 2 scripts and a shell command to 1 line of SQL: **twenty years of big data progress** in one example. The results were verified on MovieLens `ml-latest-small` (9,742 movies, 20 genres).

### SQL and DataFrames: one engine

```python
bikepoint_df.createOrReplaceTempView("BikePoints")

spark_session.sql("""
  SELECT id, commonName,
         MIN(CAST(value AS INT)) AS min_bikes,
         MAX(CAST(value AS INT)) AS max_bikes,
         ROUND(AVG(CAST(value AS INT)), 2) AS avg_bikes
  FROM BikePoints WHERE key = 'NbBikes'
  GROUP BY id, commonName""")        # → a DataFrame
```

- A **temporary view** is just a name in the session's catalog for a DataFrame's plan.
- `sql()` returns a **DataFrame**, so you can keep chaining DataFrame methods or register it again.
- `explain()` showed the **same physical plan** for SQL and the DataFrame API (lab 18.1).

![Spark UI, SQL / DataFrame tab: both APIs appear as queries (lab 18.1)](data:image/webp;base64,)

|---|---|---|---|

| **17.1** Flights EDA | MinIO `raw-flights` → `read.csv` → metadata → profiling → business questions | **605,765** flights (Jan 2008) | A reference **EDA**: `"NA"` made 14 columns strings; 7.41% of arrivals were 1 h+ late; Chicago O'Hare had 4,931 of them |
| **18.1** Spark SQL API | `bikepoint_df` → `createOrReplaceTempView` → `spark.sql` → DataFrame | **7.09%** of docks unavailable | Temporary views, SQL on DataFrames, long → wide with `SUM(CASE WHEN …)` and `PIVOT` (643 of 797 stations) |
| **11.1** Databricks edition | Unity Catalog volume → PySpark on serverless compute | **0** servers to manage | The same questions on a **managed lakehouse platform** |

Every one of these numbers was computed in class, on real data, with the tools of the course, so you can now check claims like these yourself.

### Ten traps we learnt to avoid

1. **Numbers stored as text:** min/max go alphabetical (`"13" < "9"`). **Cast** before aggregating.
2. **Missing values in disguise:** `"NA"` isn't null, and null checks said 0. Use `.option("nullValue", "NA")`.
3. **inferSchema reads the data twice:** fine for labs, but declare a schema for big data.
4. **Commas inside quotes:** `"American President, The (1995)"` broke a naive `split(",")`. Use a CSV reader or `rsplit`.
5. **Everything to the driver:** `collect()` / `toPandas()` on big data crash the driver, so `limit()` first.
6. **Only one table shows:** Jupyter displays only the last expression, so wrap each one in `display()`.
7. **"% of what?":** our percentages summed to 96.92%. Pick one denominator and say which.
8. **Tiny groups win rankings:** 9 flights at Adak → 22%. Set a minimum volume.
9. **Credentials go missing… or leak:** NiFi doesn't export secrets, and Git must never store them.
10. **Time is tricky:** hhmm integers, session time zones, and `modified` ≠ snapshot time.

Each trap came from a real lab, not a textbook. Most of them show up the same way in SQL, pandas or any cloud platform, so the habits transfer.

## 7. What's Next

### Your group assignment: an EDA checklist

1. **Land the data** in the lake with a clear name: `/<layer>/<source>/<dataset>/` or one bucket per source.
2. **Metadata:** schema, size, samples, entities, metrics, dimensions, column groups.
3. **Profile** each group: `summary()`, nulls, distinct values, most and least frequent values.
4. **Fix how you read** whatever profiling reveals: types, null markers, odd values.
5. **Answer business questions** with clear denominators and minimum volumes.
6. **Tell the story:** charts, the few numbers that matter, and what the business should do.

> **Before you submit, check:** types first · `min ≤ quartiles ≤ max` · parts add up to totals · "% of what" next to every percentage · every table matches its title. **Your reference:** lab 17.1 (Flights EDA) shows every step on real data, including the mistakes worth fixing.
